ranking.rationale: Weather condition is a strong, semantically causal driver of accident severity/risk and should transfer across domains better than calendar variables, year, or finer-grained artifacts. It captures hazardous states like rain, snow, fog, and storms more robustly than any single weather scalar alone, giving high stable marginal value as a first feature.

Junction is a strong, semantically stable road-topology signal for accident severity/risk that should transfer across domains better than time, year, or finer weather variables already partly covered by Weather_Condition; it adds complementary infrastructure information without relying on likely domain identifiers or brittle temporal shortcuts.

Traffic signals add strong, semantically stable road-structure information beyond Junction and Weather_Condition; signalized intersections materially affect accident severity/risk across domains, while being less likely than time or year features to encode domain shifts or brittle shortcuts.

Visibility is a direct, semantically causal indicator of driving hazard severity that should transfer across domains better than calendar/time variables or location-proxy road features. It adds complementary weather risk information beyond Weather_Condition while avoiding stronger domain-shift and shortcut concerns from Year, Month, Hour, or sparse infrastructure indicators.

Hour adds strong, semantically stable signal about traffic density and crash severity patterns across domains, complementing weather/visibility and road-control features without relying on likely domain identifiers like Year or brittle proxies like Minute.

Weekday adds stable behavioral exposure information beyond Hour and weather: commuting patterns and traffic mix differ systematically by day of week, and this relationship should transfer across domains better than Year/Month or finer-grained calendar fields. It is less likely to encode domain identity than Year, less redundant than Civil_Twilight given Hour, and typically more broadly predictive than sparse road-feature indicators.

Adds stable illumination information beyond Hour/Weekday and weather: day-vs-night strongly affects visibility, driver behavior, and severity risk across domains, while being less brittle than Year/Month and more semantically direct than Minute or many sparse road-feature indicators.

Crossing adds stable road-topology signal not yet covered by weather/time features; it is broadly predictive of accident risk/severity across domains and less likely than Year/Month/Day or POI-like indicators to encode dataset-specific shifts or leakage.

Precipitation adds robust weather-risk signal beyond condition and visibility, capturing rain/snow intensity that should transfer across domains better than calendar fields or sparse road-POI indicators.

Stop signs add stable road-control information not yet covered by junction/crossing/traffic-signal features, helping distinguish intersection regulation and likely severity patterns across domains. It is more semantically causal and less domain-specific than year/month/day or brittle weather residuals, and likely offers better marginal value than rarer road-feature indicators.

Temperature adds broad, semantically stable weather risk information beyond condition, visibility, and precipitation, capturing icing/heat effects that generalize across domains better than calendar fields or sparse road-feature indicators.

Month adds stable seasonal structure beyond hour/weekday and current weather, capturing recurring accident-risk patterns tied to climate, daylight, and travel behavior that should transfer across domains better than year, minute, or sparse road-POI indicators.

It adds strong, semantically stable signal about accident severity because longer affected distance generally reflects more serious incidents across domains. Unlike Year or fine-grained calendar/time fields, it is less likely to act as a domain identifier, and it complements the already selected weather, road-context, and coarse temporal features with direct incident-impact information.

Wind speed adds complementary, semantically stable weather risk beyond condition, visibility, precipitation, and temperature; it can affect vehicle control and hazard severity across domains, while being less likely than year/day/minute or sparse POI indicators to encode domain shift or brittle shortcuts.

Traffic-calming infrastructure adds stable road-design signal beyond junction/crossing/stop/traffic-signal features: it directly relates to vehicle speed and conflict patterns and should transfer across domains better than calendar fields, POI proxies, or year/minute variables that risk encoding dataset or domain artifacts.

Rail crossings are a stable roadway-context hazard signal that complements junction/crossing/signal/stop features without relying on likely domain-specific temporal or demographic shortcuts. It is more semantically tied to accident risk across regions than Year/Day/Minute and less redundant or weak than remaining weather variables and rare POI indicators.

Give-way control adds stable road-topology and right-of-way information not yet captured by the selected set. It is more semantically tied to accident risk across domains than calendar identifiers like Year/Day/Minute or brittle POI/location proxies, and it complements Junction, Stop, Traffic_Signal, and Crossing by covering another distinct intersection-control regime.

Humidity adds complementary, semantically stable weather signal beyond temperature, precipitation, visibility, wind, and condition; it can capture fog/road-surface risk without relying on likely domain-specific calendar or location artifacts.

Road bumps are a direct, location-level roadway hazard that should remain semantically predictive across domains and add complementary infrastructure signal beyond junction/crossing/stop/traffic-calming features. It is likely more stable and less domain-identifying than year, day, minute, station, or amenity, and more actionable than weaker weather residuals like pressure or wind direction.

Roundabouts encode stable road-geometry and conflict-pattern differences that plausibly affect accident severity across domains, adding complementary infrastructure signal beyond junction/crossing/stop/traffic-signal features. It is less likely than Year, Day, Minute, or POI indicators to act as a domain/time shortcut, and likely more semantically robust than pressure or wind direction once weather and visibility are already included.

Wind direction adds complementary meteorological signal beyond weather condition, precipitation, visibility, temperature, humidity, and wind speed, and its relationship to road hazard should transfer better across domains than calendar identifiers or sparse POI/location proxies. The remaining alternatives are either likely domain/time-shift markers (Year, Day, Minute), weakly informative after existing road-context features (Amenity, No_Exit, Station), or largely redundant/noisy weather summaries (Pressure).

Atmospheric pressure adds complementary weather-state information beyond visibility, precipitation, temperature, humidity, and wind, and can stably capture storm systems and hazardous driving conditions across domains. It is more semantically tied to accident risk and less likely to encode dataset-specific or temporal/domain identifiers than Year, Day, or Minute, while likely offering broader and more robust signal than sparse POI/road-feature indicators.

Amenity adds a relatively stable road-context signal about commercial or service-dense areas that can affect traffic complexity and accident risk, while being less domain-specific than Year and less redundant/noisy than Day or Minute. It is also likely more broadly informative than rarer indicators like No_Exit or Station.

Nearby stations can add modest, semantically stable signal about road environment and traffic complexity beyond junction/crossing/signal features. It is less likely than Year to encode domain shift directly, and more broadly useful than No_Exit, Day, or Minute, which are either too sparse or brittle calendar/time artifacts already largely covered by Hour, Weekday, and Month.

No_Exit adds a small but semantically stable road-topology signal about constrained street layout and maneuver options, which can generalize across domains. The remaining time-index features are more likely to capture dataset-specific temporal shifts or calendar artifacts: Year is a strong domain identifier, Day of month is weak and brittle, and Minute is usually noisy with limited stable value once Hour/Weekday/Month are included.

Day of month may add a small amount of stable calendar variation beyond month, weekday, and hour, while being less tied to benchmark split artifacts than year and less likely to capture noisy, non-semantic timestamp idiosyncrasies than minute. Year is often a strong domain identifier in WhyShift accident shifts, and minute is usually weak and brittle.

Minute may add a small amount of stable within-day timing signal beyond Hour, whereas Year is more likely to encode temporal domain shift, dataset collection changes, and non-stationary trends rather than causal accident risk. Thus Minute has higher marginal out-of-distribution value and lower leakage risk.

Year is the only remaining candidate; however, it likely captures temporal/domain shift and reporting or traffic-trend changes more than stable accident semantics, so its marginal OOD value is limited and should be weakly prioritized.
